topic: Introduction to Holomorphic Dynamics: The Beauty of Iteration
target_audience: Undergraduate students in mathematics or physics

sections.title: Prerequisites: The Complex Plane and Functions
sections.content: Review complex numbers as vectors (a + bi) and the concept of a holomorphic function as a mapping that preserves angles (conformal). Define the iteration process: f(f(f(...z...))).
sections.example: Visualizing a point z on the complex plane being 'pushed' by a function f(z) = z².

sections.title: Fixed Points and Attractors
sections.content: Introduce stable and unstable fixed points. Explain the 'Orbit' of a point under iteration. A stable fixed point acts like a gravitational sink.
sections.example: An animation of a 'Digital Magnet' (the fixed point) pulling surrounding scattered particles toward it.

sections.title: The Julia Set: Defining the Boundary of Chaos
sections.content: Explain that the Julia set is the set of points where the dynamic behavior is 'sensitive' or chaotic. Small changes in initial position lead to wildly different long-term orbits.
sections.example: A 'Tug-of-War' visual: Points inside the Julia set flee to infinity, while points outside spiral toward a central attractor.

sections.title: The Mandelbrot Set: The Map of All Dynamics
sections.content: Introduce the Mandelbrot set as the 'parameter space'—a map showing which functions f_c(z) = z² + c produce connected vs. disconnected Julia sets.
sections.example: A zoom-in animation into the Mandelbrot set showing 'mini-Mandelbrot' copies, highlighting self-similarity.

sections.title: Real-World Application: Fractal Growth
sections.content: Connect holomorphic dynamics to nature. Explain how simple recursive rules generate complex structures found in biological systems.
sections.example: A virtual 'Fractal Fern' growing: showing how iterating a simple complex function can simulate the branching patterns of biological life.
